variants.name: concurrent.futures process pool for CPU-bound sub-tasks (Python 3.2+)
variants.implementation_notes: CPython's GIL makes threads useless for CPU-bound sub-tasks, so the canonical master is a process pool: ProcessPoolExecutor (or multiprocessing.Pool) forks workers that each have their own interpreter and GIL, submit() dispatches, map(chunksize=...) dispatches and joins in input order (chunking many small items keeps IPC cheap), as_completed() joins in arrival order, and the context manager's shutdown waits for the batch. Sub-task arguments and partial results are pickled across the process boundary, so they must be importable, picklable and preferably small, and nested submission (a worker submitting to its own pool) deadlocks. ThreadPoolExecutor is only for I/O-bound sub-tasks; Python 3.14's InterpreterPoolExecutor is the new middle ground with per-interpreter GILs.
variants.code_sketch:
def run(data, workers):
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers) as pool:   # masters the worker set
        futures = [pool.submit(compute_part, lo, hi)          # dispatch
                   for lo, hi in partition(data, workers)]
        parts = [f.result() for f in futures]                 # join (in order)
    return combine(parts)                                     # combine
pitfalls: Everything crosses a pickle boundary: lambdas, closures and large payloads fail or are copied; pass module-level callables and chunk small items explicitly.
A worker submitting to the same pool deadlocks (documented for both executors) - flatten the fan-out instead of nesting it.
Pure-Python CPU work on ThreadPoolExecutor is serial because of the GIL, so choosing threads silently removes the parallelism.
Pool startup and shutdown are not free: reuse one executor across phases, and note that pending futures still run unless cancel_futures is requested.

variants.name: asyncio.TaskGroup for I/O-bound fan-out (Python 3.11+)
variants.implementation_notes: asyncio.TaskGroup is the structured-concurrency master: tasks created inside the async with block are the dispatched children, leaving the block is the join, and the first exception cancels the remaining children (untasked gather() instead lets the others keep running). Keep strong references to the task objects - the event loop holds only weak ones, so an unreferenced task can be garbage-collected mid-flight - and never run blocking sub-tasks directly in a coroutine; move them to a thread or process executor with loop.run_in_executor or asyncio.to_thread. asyncio is single-threaded, so this realization is for many I/O-bound sub-tasks, not for CPU work.
variants.code_sketch:
async def run(n: int) -> list[Partial]:
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:        # master: join at block exit
        tasks = [tg.create_task(compute_part(i)) for i in range(n)]
    return [t.result() for t in tasks]           # combine after the join
pitfalls: TaskGroup cancels the remaining children on the first failure - catch inside the child or use gather when every partial must survive.
Tasks without a strong reference may be garbage-collected before completion (documented warning): keep them in a collection until awaited.
Blocking calls (time.sleep, requests, file I/O) stall the whole loop; offload them with to_thread or run_in_executor.
asyncio gives concurrency, not parallelism: CPU-bound sub-tasks belong in a process pool.
